mitigation_mechanism: Mangrove stems and roots dissipate wave energy, lowering wave height behind the belt.
caveats: Graded on the register band for percent change (31% > 30% = strong). Field measurements in natural mangroves, not restored stands; mangroves were the weakest of the four habitats; effect depends on water depth and vegetation height.
justification: Narayan et al. (2016). The Effectiveness, Costs and Coastal Protection Benefits of Natural and Nature-Based Defences. PLOS ONE. — p.4: "Coral reefs reduce wave heights by 70% (95% CI: 54–81%), salt-marshes by 72% (95%CI: 62–79%), mangroves by 31% (95% CI: 25–37%) and seagrass/kelp beds by 36% (95% CI: 25– 45%)."

mitigation_mechanism: Wind and swell waves are rapidly dissipated as they pass through mangroves, lessening wave damage during storms.
caveats: Synthesis states the effect as rapid (strong); elsewhere the same report gives 13-66% wave-height reduction per 100 m. Needs hundreds of metres of belt.
justification: Spalding, M., McIvor, A., Tonneijck, F. H., Tol, S., and van Eijk, P. (2014). Mangroves for coastal defence. Guidelines for coastal managers & policy makers. Wetlands International and The Nature Conservancy. — p.8: "Wind and swell waves are rapidly reduced as they pass through mangroves, lessening wave damage during storms."

mitigation_mechanism: Wide mangrove belts slow storm-surge water as it moves inland, reducing flood depth and extent in low-lying land behind them.
caveats: Coastal storm-surge flooding only. Needs belts thousands of metres wide; surge reduction per km is small (5-50 cm) but can greatly reduce flooded area. Not a stand-alone defence.
justification: Spalding, M., McIvor, A., Tonneijck, F. H., Tol, S., and van Eijk, P. (2014). Mangroves for coastal defence. Guidelines for coastal managers & policy makers. Wetlands International and The Nature Conservancy. — p.18: "While storm surge depths may only be reduced by 5-50 cm per kilometre width of mangroves, nevertheless a small reduction in water level can already greatly reduce the extent of flooding in low lying areas behind the mangroves."

mitigation_mechanism: Restored mangrove area added to coastal flood models reduces the number of people flooded each year.
caveats: Modelled global total for full restoration of mapped loss areas; no per-hectare effect size, so graded by the narrative rule (low).
justification: Worthington, T., and Spalding, M. (2018). Mangrove Restoration Potential: A global map highlighting a critical opportunity. The Nature Conservancy, IUCN and University of Cambridge. — p.4: "Full restoration of the areas identified could enable: o Carbon sequestration in aboveground biomass amounting to 69 million tonnes of carbon, equivalent to annual emissions from 25,000,000 US homes; o The saving of 296 million tonnes of soil carbon stocks through a combination of avoided emissions and sequestration emissions, equivalent to annual emissions from 117,000,000 US homes; o The addition of commercial fisheries species in mangrove waters totalling 23 trillion young-of-year finfish and 40 trillion crabs, shrimp and molluscs; and o Protection from annual coastal flooding for hundreds of thousands of people."

mitigation_mechanism: Severe storm winds and waves can break or uproot mangrove trees.
caveats: Two fragments of one sentence, split by a page header in the text layer; quoted separately, not stitched.
justification: Spalding, M., McIvor, A., Tonneijck, F. H., Tol, S., and van Eijk, P. (2014). Mangroves for coastal defence. Guidelines for coastal managers & policy makers. Wetlands International and The Nature Conservancy. — p.18: "In the most severe storms, mangroves may themselves be damaged or torn up" | p.18: "by the high winds and waves, although breakage or uprooting of mangrove trees is relatively rare."
